title: Austrian and Swiss women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
description: Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian – have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city o
body: Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian – have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.Swiss national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Austrian Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi.It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah. Niger and the broader Sahel region have faced years of jihadist violence, including kidnappings and deadly attacks, carried out by different groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State.The country has been under military control since 2023 when Gen Abdourahmane Tchiani deposed the country's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum.

schema.headline: Austrian and Swiss women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya

title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
description: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.A judge in New Mexico on
body: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data."The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too. Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times."For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday. "Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional. Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021. Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people. "Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said.  To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn.The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents.Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.Meta's revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn.Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta's chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock. Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use "more funding flexibility" next year.

schema.headline: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy

title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots for political gain
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the countryByPatrick JacksonMarco Silva an
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the countryByPatrick JacksonMarco Silva and Thomas CopelandBBC Verify French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the  riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.   The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools. Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders... "We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France. "When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country.""Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron.According to a report in the UK's Financial Times newspaper, external, EU regulators are examining possible foreign online interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and similar recent outbursts of unrest in EU states.It quotes unnamed security officials as saying that pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos.Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, the paper adds.David Colon, a researcher at France's Sciences Po university who specialises in disinformation, was quoted as saying that "pro-Kremlin influencers" linked to the Russian campaign Storm-1516 had "amplified the events and spread a number of false narratives".France is one of Ukraine's most vociferous military supporters in its ongoing war with Russia, while Algeria is a former French colony with bitter memories of its war to achieve independence in 1962, and French relations with Iran have been strained by its war with the US and Israel this year.         BBC Verify has reviewed more than 15 examples of fake news videos on social media which researchers at the US-based dTeam say are the work of a Russian disinformation operation known as Matryoshka.The videos feature near-identical branding to real news outlets in France, including Le Monde, Euronews and France 24.The individual impact and reach of videos made by Matryoshka appear to be limited, but experts have said the focus on amplifying unrest is consistent with known Russian disinformation tactics.Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image.It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened.While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views.Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated.

schema.headline: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots for political gain

title: Mexico ex-prosecutor charged with treason over US drug raid
description: Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in Ap
body: Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April without proper authorisation.César Jáuregui Moreno served as attorney general of the northern border state of Chihuahua from 2023 to this year.The involvement of Americans came to light after two US agents said to have worked for the CIA died in a car crash in Chihuahua along with two Mexican law enforcement officers.  Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said Jáuregui had allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and had failed to share information. Jáuregui has denied the allegations.The former prosecutor, who is a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A court hearing is scheduled for Saturday. A judge must still determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed with the case, Reuters news agency reports.Jáuregui also faces state-level charges in Chihuahua, including of abuse of public office. In a court hearing for those charges on Sunday, he denied that he instructed or consented to the involvement of US agents in the operation.Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has come under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on drug trafficking but has repeatedly declined offers of US-led counter-narcotics operations in the country.She has been adamant that foreign officials can only operate on Mexican soil if given prior clearance by the federal government, and has insisted the Latin American nation's sovereignty should not be breached.The crash occurred on 19 April, when a convoy returning from an operation targeting suspected methamphetamine labs in a remote, mountainous area veered off the road and plunged into a ravine. Two members of the Chihuahua State Investigation Agency were killed along with the Americans, officials said.At the time, in his capacity as state attorney general, Jáuregui told a news conference that the Americans had been "instructor officers" from the US embassy engaged in "training work as part of the general and normal exchange we have with the US authorities".US media have reported that the two individuals worked for the CIA as part of an expanded effort to combat narcotics trafficking in the region.

schema.headline: Mexico ex-prosecutor charged with treason over US drug raid

title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
description: Image caption, Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's electionByYolande KnellMiddle East corre
body: Image caption, Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's electionByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromNazarethAt rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties."I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."Image caption, All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab partiesMost opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.Image caption, Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity.  Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.Image caption, Radio Nas anchor Mohammed Magadli says Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to delegitimise Arab partiesAt Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party. I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties."In a word its racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings. These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.Image caption, United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas wants Arab parties to reach a "position of influence"While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc. For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government."We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me. "That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Joint List talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace Netanyahu's governmentMeanwhile, the Joint List - which is made up of secular parties and advocates for equal rights for Arab Israelis, an end to Israeli military occupation of Palestinian territories, and a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict - aims to wield a position of influence within the opposition. It talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace the Netanyahu government, in return for support on important policies.A main issue in this election for Arab Israelis is rampant gang crime. In September, a poll by the Israel Democracy Institute think tank found that this was the most important factor for 53.5% of Arab citizens when deciding which party to vote for. Murders within the community reached a record high of 252 last year – about five times higher than the number of Jewish Israelis who were killed, according to the Abraham Initiatives, a Jewish-Arab organisation that promotes coexistence.Image caption, Arab Israelis accuse the government of inaction on the issue of gang crimeIn Jaffa, a mixed Arab-Jewish neighbourhood which is now joined to Tel Aviv, Ziad Samouni shows me where his son, Hussein, was shot dead by two gunmen on a motorcycle near his home last November. No arrests have been made in his case. With a low percentage of cases solved, Arab-Israelis accuse the government of inaction."It seems they're interested in making sure we reach a situation where the killer is never caught, allowing Arabs in Arab society to keep killing one another," says Samouni, who is now part of a support group, Israeli-Palestinian Bereaved Families for Peace.The Israeli police told the BBC its investigation into Hussein's murder remained active, adding that it took "every case of violence and crime with the utmost seriousness.""As a father who's lost a son, of course, I want this bloodshed to end," Samouni tells me. "I wish every Arab citizen who believes there needs to be a change sees that this is a time to go to vote."Image source, Ziad SamouniImage caption, Ziad Samouni's son Hussein (2nd L) was shot dead last November but no arrests have been made This month, Israel's Supreme Court overruled a decision by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify the United Arab List and the Joint List as well as two of their members.The committee, which is dominated by the governing coalition, argued that they broke a law banning candidates who deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish state. The parties and their representatives strongly denied it.With just days to go before voting, back in Nazareth, some motorists display flags for their preferred party on their cars.The stakes are high in this election: Arab citizens could yet decide who wields power in Israel, and they also see this vote as key to their own future in the country.

schema.headline: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election

title: Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say
description: Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for
body: Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for a holiday, the head of Africa's health agency has told the BBC.The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, where she fell ill three days after arriving home in the Nigerian capital on 3 October, according to Dr Jean Kaseya from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.Nigeria's health minister has confirmed to the BBC the 42-year-old patient spent two and a half weeks in Kampala, adding that she also made a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return."She's stable, she's improving," Muhammad Ali Pate said.The authorities were working to prevent the virus from spreading and had identified 44 people who had been in contact with the woman, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, the minister said."Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible," Pate told the BBC.None of the contacts, who are now in isolation, are known to have developed symptoms, including the person the patient travelled with, the health minister said, adding that the woman had not travelled outside Abuja since landing.Kaseya explained that the woman had first developed symptoms on 6 October when she had sought medical help."She went to the first hospital, a private hospital, thinking that she had malaria, and then she went to the second private hospital. She was admitted on the 11th," he told the BBC's Newshour programme.Malaria is endemic in Nigeria and its symptoms - a high temperature, headaches, muscle aches, vomiting and or diarrhoea - are similar to those of Ebola.After her condition failed to improve, public health authorities were alerted on Monday 19 October, Pate said.Her diagnosis was confirmed the next day following three laboratory tests, he said.The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded,  the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external.Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.There have been conflicting accounts about the patient in Nigeria and her movements.Pate and Kaseya's comments contradict a statement issued earlier by the Ugandan ministry of health, which described the woman as a Nigerian national who had gone to eastern DR Congo for business, only transiting through Uganda.It insisted there were currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country and that the woman's passage through Uganda did not mean she had contracted the virus there.Nigeria's health minister and the Africa CDC chief have sought to play down any tension.Pate said Nigerian officials were working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the full facts."We respect our sister nation of Uganda," he said. "We have very strong solidarity, we are all in it together."Kaseya also urged African countries to share information, saying this would help investigators trace the woman's movements and establish where she might have contracted the virus.And he encouraged Western countries not to impose travel restrictions, saying "collaboration and solidarity" were the way to help stop the current outbreak.The disease recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.In 2014, Nigeria successfully contained an Ebola outbreak, which had resulted in 20 confirmed cases and eight deaths.Pate expressed confidence in the country's ability to repeat that success, citing strengthened disease surveillance, laboratories and thousands of trained epidemiologists."Nigeria has muscle memory that has been activated, but we are not fighting the past outbreak in the exactly the same way. We have to be vigilant," he said.The outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.Additional reporting by Timothy Obiezu and Lucy Fleming

schema.headline: Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say

title: Orient beach attack: South African swimmer killed by shark
description: A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.Janine Loc
body: A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London"."She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave."She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

schema.headline: Orient beach attack: South African swimmer killed by shark

title: CJP protest: India 'cockroach' leaders who called on election chief to quit are freed from jail
description: The CJP is not a registered political party, but a collective which began by mobilising thousands of young people to protest over leaked exam papers.
body: The CJP is not a registered political party, but a collective which began by mobilising thousands of young people to protest over leaked exam papers. By July it had emerged as a major force.A march towards parliament that month ended in clashes with police, drawing wider attention to the movement and increasing pressure on the government. The unrest eventually led to the resignation of India's education minister.The CJP has since shifted its focus to India's electoral system. Along with opposition parties, students and other critics of the government, it accuses Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar of revising electoral rolls, an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the allegation.The SIR exercise has resulted in around 130 million names being removed from voter lists since last year.Critics warn that the process could also exclude eligible voters, potentially denying them their right to vote, while the Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove ineligible, dead and duplicate entries.Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external Twitter, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: CJP protest: India 'cockroach' leaders who called on election chief to quit are freed from jail

title: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
description: Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.  "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk sa
body: Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.  "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move."The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.    That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.SpaceX, as a whole is not profitable, despite revenue jumping to $27bn from $13.7bn over the first nine months of the year.Over that same period it lost $1.1bn although it did report a $4.4bn profit for the most recent three months.Following Musk's comments, SpaceX's share price rose 8% in after-hours trading. Shares in Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose by 2% Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence and software.

schema.headline: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX

title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
description: For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a p
body: For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.But that may end soon.Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally."Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business. A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level."A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders. Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants". While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible. While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP). Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies."This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work."Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

schema.headline: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream

title: Aichi-Nagoya: Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByKurumi MoriTokyo correspondent and Issey IzumiFrom the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a stron
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByKurumi MoriTokyo correspondent and Issey IzumiFrom the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected."If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.String of incidentsBefore the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds".Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000. Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Container units were used to host some participants as organisers opted not to build a traditional athletes' villageThis was just the start of the problems.Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations."Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said."During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Organisers acknowledged major challenges and said athletes from some delegations had been inconvenienced'Overwhelmingly cheaper'As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games"."We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given."Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.Image source, China News Service/VCG via Getty ImagesImage caption, Volunteers were told they could attend the closing ceremony for free, before an organiser said that decision hadn't been approvedHopes for the futureWatching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit."This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

schema.headline: Aichi-Nagoya: Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic

title: Alberta's decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump
description: "Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red an
body: "Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners.It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada.But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province.Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world.Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief – at home, and beyond its borders.Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too."Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome.Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world".Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south – in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state.The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls."I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding."For Canadians, it's no laughing matter.In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" – even if he didn't spell out who "they" is.He didn't have to.And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer – including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific.But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast."Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding director of the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto."Foreign investors are focused on the time it will take to complete major infrastructure projects, a return on investment, and predictable regulations," she explains in a nod to Carney's long list of megaprojects he hopes will eventually turbocharge economic growth. They're all costly; many will take years to build.An ambitious blueprint already includes a proposed pipeline to the Pacific coast which opens opportunities for Alberta's oil to reach Asian markets – a move which also addresses Alberta's long-standing grievance that its economy has been stifled by federal policies, including environmental regulations.At a rally in Alberta last week, it was Carney's comment that the pipeline "will reduce our dependence on the United States" that triggered the loudest and longest applause of the night.After Monday's vote, Carney – the former UN Special Envoy for Climate Action and Finance –   pointed to "unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta as its core". Political and economic pressures now seem to eclipse his green credentials."Build Canada Strong" has been Carney's mantra ever since he first entered politics, a complete neophyte, at the start of last year.At home there are possible wide-reaching repercussions from the final tallies in the referendum's nine other questions which dealt with issues ranging from greater provincial powers, the costs of immigration, and potential constitutional changes.Those results are certain to provoke debate, and deal making or breaking, involving Canada's nine other provinces and three territories. They all have their own grievances, too.The prime minister has had to defend himself when journalists ask if he is spending too much time on foreign trips with his charm offensive to build new political alliances and trade partnerships, including an unprecedented and still uncertain offer of associate membership of the European Union."I can do both and I need to do both," he recently replied with his signature bluntness before listing the more than 16 bills which went through Parliament in the last session dealing with everything from major tax changes, public safety, and the price of fuel.For now, Carney is riding high in the polls at home – including in Alberta, which doesn't traditionally support his Liberal party - in a long "political honeymoon" other beleaguered politicians would envy.And the plain-speaking politician's strong and steady response to Trump threats, including retaliatory tariffs, has seen his star rising on the world stage. It's an unexpected turn for a country which has often been missing from top tables and has sometimes even been dismissed as "boring".The Economist magazine decided to put Carney on their cover, on this week of weeks for Canada, with a perfect red maple leaf between his teeth."Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world," reads one of its headlines, with an article which also focuses on Canada's "vulnerabilities" including Alberta's ballot."The broader takeaway from this vote might be that Canadian unity is in fine shape," remarks David Moscrop, political scientist and author of the forthcoming book On Nationalism."But what happens after Donald Trump is gone and Canada no longer has a single, bombastic target which drives Canadians to rally around the flag?" he asks.Carney's decision to recently walk away from trade talks with the US gave rise to another swell of Canadian pride and patriotism. But if this trade war drags on with a country which traditionally takes 70% of Canada's exports, Canadians will feel even greater pain in their daily lives.But today is a day to vigorously wave the maple leaf flag."It's a win for Team Canada and its resilience," commented CBC journalist Janyce McGregor during the public broadcaster's rolling coverage.

schema.headline: Alberta's decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump

title: Haitian migrants changed this town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again
description: Image caption, Springfield, in south-west Ohio, was thrust into the spotlight in 2024 when Trump repeated a false claim about Haitian immigrants eatin
body: Image caption, Springfield, in south-west Ohio, was thrust into the spotlight in 2024 when Trump repeated a false claim about Haitian immigrants eating petsByTom Bateman reporting from OhioIn this closely fought midterm election campaign, the small town of Springfield, Ohio, has become a symbol of modern America. But it is a symbol that changes dramatically depending on who is describing it.To President Donald Trump, Springfield crystallises America's problems due to years of unchecked immigration. He once echoed a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets here. Today, he says his mass deportation drive means its people are "getting their town back".But to others, Springfield represents a well-known cycle in the story of modern America. The decline of traditional industry, followed by a spike in immigration fuelled by cheap housing and low-paid labour. It is a familiar tale across the country.This story contains some distressing detailsPierre Damas Bel, 20, arrived in Springfield to join his father and stepmother in 2024. He fled his native Haiti, which was gripped by political instability and gang warfare. He entered the US with the government's permission under a now-defunct Biden-era programme for migrants waiting in Mexico.Bel, according to a family friend, then received a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which gives vetted individuals the right to live and work in the United States. TPS usually lasts 18 months but is routinely rolled over, often for years, if the danger remains in the affected country.Bel aspired to build a life in America, the friend said. He was an honours student, talented athlete and cadet in a high school programme training students to become officers in the US Armed Forces.But in June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US. Image caption, Pierre Damas Bel's family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear an ankle monitorBel was told to report to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office where he was fitted with an ankle monitor which is used to track migrants facing deportation.He wrote on Instagram that he felt "shame and humiliation" at having to wear the tag. And on 31 August, he parked his car on the side of a highway near Springfield, walked into oncoming traffic and was killed.His family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear the ankle monitor.The Department for Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to questions from the BBC about Bel's case.  ICE has previously rejected "any attempt to blame ICE for the death"."Remaining in the country illegally, while fighting removal, is a choice. Leaving with a free flight home and $2,600 is also a choice," a spokesperson told US media earlier this year when asked about the case.In the weeks before his death, Bel attended a Springfield support centre for Haitians facing deportation.Its co-founder, Viles Dorsainvil, told the BBC that Bel had been in the process of filing a motion asking ICE to remove the tag. "He went twice to the ICE facilities… begging them to remove the ankle monitor," he said. "He did everything right to be here until they put the tag on him."In total, more than a million immigrants from 13 countries have had TPS terminated by the Trump administration. The changes meant many went from being legal to unauthorised migrants overnight.In 2024, Trump made securing the border and the mass deportation of undocumented migrants core pledges in his election campaign. Polls suggest the border policy continues to have strong support among Republicans, but the nature of his immigration enforcement campaign has seen a drop in backing this year.Figure caption, Watch: How Trump's mass deportation drive is playing out in OhioOhio has become a swing state in the coming midterm Congressional elections, and one of two Republican-held Senate seats is up for grabs. Trump has visited the state twice already in an attempt to rally turnout and counter a slide in his approval ratings.At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, earlier this month, Trump returned to the topic of Springfield."You have a little town, beautiful little town in Ohio where they dropped about 35,000 Haitians. Well, they're being taken out and they're almost going to be gone and we're giving their town back," he said to cheers.The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled in its favour in the summer."The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY, yet many of these designations became de facto amnesty," James Percival, the general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said after the court's ruling. "This is a win for the rule of law and common sense."In a social media post in August, the Department of Homeland Security posted a video of Haitians in chains wearing white uniforms being led onto a deportation flight. The video, accompanied by jaunty music, told Haitians whose TPS had expired to "LEAVE IMMEDIATELY".The Trump administration has said it is conducting law enforcement operations in the town to keep Americans safe. It has also argued that Haiti is safe enough to return to.The country is subject to the US State Department's highest Level 4 "Do Not Travel" danger warning.GUIDE: What are the US midterms?EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midtermsIN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightropeThe signs of decades of economic decline are still visible in Springfield, through shuttered factories and boarded up homes. This part of the American Midwest was hit badly by last century's de-industrialisation, when those laid off from its once prolific factories sought work on the coasts or migrated to warmer, southern states.Within the last five years, a Haitian population estimated to be around 20,000 strong arrived in the town. Many fled the devastating earthquake in 2010. Others left Haiti in 2021 during the violence and unrest that followed President Jovenel Moise's assassination.It meant Springfield's population increased rapidly. With their legal status under TPS, many Haitians took on low-paid jobs in factories and distribution warehouses.Image caption, Rick Johnson is a strong supporter of ICE's deportation driveRick Johnson, who served in the Marines, has a porch adorned with flags. The Stars and Stripes flutter close to a banner for the US Navy and another for the Marine Corps.Johnson's wife served in the Navy while he was in the Marines at Camp Pendleton in California. Outside of his service, he has lived in Springfield his whole life. He made it clear he is a strong supporter of ICE's deportation drive."You get where we're coming from," he said. "We love America, we love Americans - any kind of Americans, but you kind of have to be American."Johnson moved into this neighbourhood a decade ago, but he said the loss of industry has left much of it empty. "They've torn down every house around me, I don't really have any neighbours," he said. "The only neighbours I have are Haitians right here and they don't really bother me."They moved in around four years ago, Johnson added, "but there's a lot of them".  He referenced "the driving problems".This is a view shared by other residents in Springfield - a perception that traffic accidents increased after the Haitian community arrived. In 2023, an 11-year-old boy, Aiden Clark, was killed when his school bus overturned in a crash with a minivan. The van driver, Herman Joseph, originally from Haiti, did not have a valid US driver's licence and was jailed.Aiden's father, Nathan Clark, later spoke at a Springfield City Commission meeting where he denounced politicians for using his son's death as a "political tool" to fuel anti-immigrant sentiment, saying his son was accidentally killed.Johnson's concern is about the numbers and the speed of change. "Really it's the amount of them," he told the BBC. "If you come here you [should] come here legally. The Temporary Protected Status is done… it's time to go."Image caption, Within the last five years, a Haitian population estimated to be around 20,000-strong arrived in SpringfieldAt a nearby grocery store run by Paschur Castelly, who left Haiti 20 years ago, most of the shelves are empty, except for those stocking religious candles and framed pictures of Catholic saints popular with this devout community."I can't purchase new merchandise because I don't have people coming in," he said."So, our communities, we have doctors, we have engineers… we came here to get a better life, to help our family in Haiti, you know? Our country doesn't offer us security."After 20 minutes in the store, the first customer arrived. The man, who asked to remain anonymous, said he had been a warehouse worker for three years.But like others who have lost TPS, it is likely to mean he has also lost the right to work. As he chatted with Castelly, he pulled up his right trouser leg and revealed a large ankle monitor. ICE has said these are part of its Alternatives to Detention programme. "I was given a choice, wear the ankle monitor and report in every two weeks, or sign my deportation order," he said.As we left the store, Castelly closed the door which he now keeps locked. When a neighbour spotted us and feared an ICE raid, she shouted over to ask if Castelly was okay.It was a sign of just how much this town remains a symbol - of two versions of America - years after Trump thrust it into the national spotlight, and weeks before voters head to the polls to shape the remainder of his presidency.With additional reporting by Gringo WotshelaIf you're affected by any of the issues in this article you can find details of organisations who can help via the BBC Action Line.Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external, external.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Haitian migrants changed this town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again

title: Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capitalByPaul AdamsDiplomatic correspondentThe hug that Trump envoy Steve Wi
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capitalByPaul AdamsDiplomatic correspondentThe hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.Just listen to the way they talk about each other."Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.The verbal assault has continued this week."Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, using an expletive while criticising Benjamin Netanyahu's judgement. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister"."Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever."We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?In some ways, we've been here before.After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.Figure caption, Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says TrumpLast Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin."What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC."It's inexplicable and saddening."Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking."We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink.A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.Image source, EPAImage caption, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabatedA decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things.""There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink."I think we will have good results too," he said.Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

schema.headline: Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism

title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate

body: "The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement. "Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

schema.headline: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
